mappings.review_reason: Biliary excretory clearance is distinct from hepatic metabolic and intrinsic clearance.
CYP-mediated metabolism is a distinct enzyme-family process; enzyme and assay context preserve its subtype.
The only row reports an elimination rate in clearance units, but does not establish equivalence to hepatic or metabolic clearance.
The Fh source rows explicitly describe hepatic extraction ratio; fraction or percent units preserve scale.
FMO-mediated metabolism is distinct from CYP- and UGT-mediated pathways.
Organ-level hepatic clearance remains distinct from intrinsic clearance, extraction ratio, and route-dependent oral clearance.
Both rows report the fraction or percentage extracted by the liver, synonymous with hepatic extraction ratio.
Reviewed embedded-space corruption of hepatic first-pass metabolism.
Hepatic first-pass metabolism and availability remain separate from extraction ratio because reported values may use opposite Fh and extraction conventions.
Whole-cell hepatocyte stability is distinct from microsomal and S9 stability, especially when assay context is missing.
Intrinsic clearance excludes flow and binding effects and must remain separate from observed hepatic or metabolic clearance.
Metabolic clearance can be non-hepatic or apparent CL/F and is not safely interchangeable with hepatic clearance.
Rows include systemic terminal half-life as well as in-vitro half-life, so this broad source endpoint remains separate from assay-specific stability.
Microsomal stability is a defined subcellular assay and remains separate from hepatocyte and S9 stability.
Oral apparent clearance is route- and bioavailability-dependent and must not merge with hepatic or intrinsic clearance.
Broad parent-drug stability rows span several biological preparations, including records with missing assay context, so they remain fail-closed.
S9 stability includes cytosolic and microsomal activity and remains distinct from either component alone.
Substrate depletion may report disappearance, rate, or change versus control and cannot safely merge with percent-remaining stability.
UGT-mediated glucuronidation is a distinct enzyme-family process from CYP and FMO metabolism.
